intro/hello: This lecture is about direct preference optimization, or D P O.
intro/recall: In the last chapter, we taught a language model from human preferences with a three stage pipeline.
intro/stages: First, supervised fine tuning. Then a reward model, trained on pairs of answers. Then P P O, pushing the model toward high reward.
intro/heavy: That last stage is heavy. Four networks in memory, fresh text sampled at every step, and a long list of settings that all have to be right.
intro/paper: In 2023, Rafailov and colleagues at Stanford showed that the last two stages can be replaced by one ordinary loss on the preference pairs.
intro/same: No reward model. No reinforcement learning loop. No sampling during training. And yet it optimizes the very same objective.
intro/title: The subtitle of their paper says it all: your language model is secretly a reward model.
intro/plan: The whole idea is five steps of algebra. We will walk them slowly, with code beside every step.
intro/toy: And we will use one tiny example throughout. One prompt: how do I reverse a list in Python?
intro/answers: Four possible answers. A is short and correct. B is correct, but rambling. C is confidently wrong. And D refuses.
intro/reward: Our pretend labelers follow a hidden reward, in gold. They like A best, and D least.
intro/ref: The reference model, in orange, is the fine tuned model we start from. It prefers the rambling answer, B.
bt/pair: Start with one comparison. A labeler sees two answers, and picks one.
bt/names: We call the chosen answer y w, for winner, and the rejected one y l, for loser.
bt/bt: The Bradley-Terry model says that each answer has a hidden score: its reward.
bt/sig: The chance that the labeler picks y w is the sigmoid of the difference between the two rewards.
bt/curve: The sigmoid squashes any number into a probability. A gap of zero gives a coin flip: one half.
bt/gap: A versus C has a reward gap of two point four, so the labeler picks A about ninety two percent of the time. Never a hundred: people are noisy.
bt/diff: Notice that only the difference matters. Add the same number to both rewards, and nothing changes.
bt/rm: In R L H F, a reward model is trained by minimizing minus the log of this probability, over many labeled pairs.
bt/keep: Keep this equation in mind. The whole derivation ends right back here.
objective/goal: Next, the objective that R L H F is really optimizing.
objective/policy: The policy, in blue, is the model we train. It gives every possible answer a probability.
objective/reward: We want its expected reward to be high: the average reward of the answers it would write.
objective/greedy: But reward alone would pile all the probability onto one answer. In practice, that is often an answer that exploits a flaw in the reward model.
objective/leash: So we add a leash. The K L divergence measures how far the policy has drifted from the reference.
objective/kl: It averages the log ratio, the log of pi over pi ref, over the policy's own answers. It is zero when the two match, and positive otherwise.
objective/beta: Beta is the price of drifting. The objective is the expected reward, minus beta times the K L.
objective/tug: Watch the tug of war. Moving probability toward A earns reward, but every step away from the orange bars costs K L. The best policy sits somewhere in between.
objective/ppo: P P O finds that policy by trial and error. D P O will find it with algebra.
optimal/surprise: Here is the surprise that makes everything work. For one prompt, this objective has an exact solution. You can simply write it down.
optimal/steps: Step one was the objective. Step two is its answer.
optimal/tilt: Take the reference model's probabilities, and multiply each one by e to the reward over beta.
optimal/grow: High reward answers grow. Low reward answers shrink.
optimal/norm: Then divide by the total, so the probabilities add up to one again. That total is called Z.
optimal/result: The result is pi star, the best possible policy. With beta equal to one, A rises to zero point three seven, while B stays on top at zero point five five.
optimal/beta: Now loosen the leash. As beta shrinks, pi star piles onto the best answer, A. Tighten it, and pi star stays close to the reference.
optimal/why: Why is this the best? Rewrite the objective, and it becomes a fixed ceiling, beta log Z, minus beta times the K L from the policy to pi star.
optimal/zero: That K L is zero only when the policy equals pi star. So nothing can beat it.
optimal/catch: There is one catch. For a real language model, Z is a sum over every possible answer: more strings than there are atoms in the universe. Nobody can compute it.
invert/back: Step three. The formula turns a reward into a policy. Read it backwards, and it turns a policy into a reward.
invert/logs: Take the log of both sides, and solve for r.
invert/result: The reward is beta times the log ratio, log of pi star over pi ref, plus beta times log Z.
invert/implicit: The first part is called the implicit reward. An answer the policy made more likely than the reference did gets a positive implicit reward.
invert/bars: Here are the true rewards in gold, and the implicit rewards in purple.
invert/shift: Every purple bar sits below its gold bar by the same amount: beta log Z, about zero point six nine here.
invert/secret: So a policy is a reward model in disguise. That is the secret in the title of the paper.
invert/stuck: But we still cannot compute Z. Luckily, look at what it is: one number per prompt, shared by every answer to that prompt.
cancel/step4: Step four. Bradley-Terry never uses a reward on its own. It only uses the difference between two rewards, for the same prompt.
cancel/sub: So substitute step three for both rewards in the pair.
cancel/two: Each one brings its own beta log Z of x. And since the prompt is the same, the two are identical.
cancel/left: What is left is the sigmoid of beta times the log ratio of the chosen answer, minus beta times the log ratio of the rejected one.
cancel/gone: The unknown reward is gone. The impossible normalizer is gone. Everything that remains is a log probability under one of two models.
cancel/check: We can check it on the toy. Shift every reward up or down by the same amount. Z changes, but pi star and every preference probability stay exactly the same.
cancel/never: Rewards were never unique anyway. A constant per prompt changes no preference, so no data could ever have pinned it down.
loss/step5: Step five turns all of this into a training rule.
loss/replace: Replace pi star with the model we are actually training, pi theta.
loss/likely: Then ask how likely our labeled pairs are under this model, and make that likelihood as large as possible.
loss/loss: That is the D P O loss: minus the log sigmoid of the implicit reward margin.
loss/margin: The margin is beta times the gap between the two log ratios: how much more the model has raised the chosen answer than the rejected one, compared with the reference.
loss/classify: This is plain binary classification: the logistic loss from the linear classifier chapter. The score is the margin, and the label is always: the first answer won.
loss/curve: Here is the loss for one pair, as the margin changes.
loss/start: Training starts with the policy equal to the reference. Every margin is zero, and the loss is log two, about zero point six nine three. That is the first line of every D P O training log.
loss/right: Rank the pair correctly, and the loss flattens toward zero. Rank it wrongly, and the loss climbs in a straight line.
loss/same: And if the model could represent any policy, the minimum of this loss is exactly pi star. Same goal as R L H F. No reward model. No reinforcement learning.
gradient/diff: Now differentiate the loss, and something readable appears.
gradient/up: Every step pushes the log probability of the chosen answer up,
gradient/down: and the log probability of the rejected answer down.
gradient/weight: But each pair is scaled by a weight: the sigmoid of minus the margin.
gradient/wrong: When the implicit reward ranks a pair the wrong way round, the weight is close to one. That pair pulls hard.
gradient/right: When the pair is already ranked correctly by a wide margin, the weight fades toward zero. That pair stops pulling.
gradient/batch: Here is a mini batch of six pairs. The last one is a noisy label that contradicts the first. At the start, every margin is zero and every weight is one half.
gradient/steps: Take a few steps. Pairs the model already gets right fade out, while the two contradicting pairs keep pulling against each other.
gradient/naive: The D P O paper notes that a naive version, without this weight, can make the model degenerate. It keeps pushing on pairs it has already won.
gradient/nosample: And notice what the gradient never needs: a sample from the policy. This is supervised learning, with a cleverly chosen loss.
beta/twice: Beta appears twice, and both times it says the same thing.
beta/obj: In the objective, it is the price of drifting away from the reference.
beta/small: A small beta is a loose leash: pi star piles onto the answer with the highest reward.
beta/large: A large beta is a short leash: pi star barely moves from the reference.
beta/loss: In the loss, beta is the exchange rate between log ratios and reward.
beta/stretch: The loss is mostly satisfied once the margin is a few units. So the log ratios have to move by a few units, divided by beta.
beta/example: With beta at zero point one, a margin of three needs a gap of thirty: an enormous change in probability. With beta at one, a gap of three will do.
beta/typical: Most runs use a value near zero point one, the default in the D P O paper.
beta/price: But remember: beta is a price, not a wall. Later, we will see a case where D P O walks right past it.
run/test: Time to test the whole claim, end to end.
run/data: We sample a thousand preference pairs once, from the reference model, and label them with a noisy labeler that follows the hidden rewards.
run/init: The policy starts as a copy of the reference. The dashed outline is pi star: the answer R L H F is looking for.
run/loop: Then we train the policy with the D P O loss and Adam.
run/never: The loop never sees a reward, and never generates a single answer.
run/watch: Watch the blue bars. A climbs, B gives way, and the wrong answer and the refusal fade out.
run/land: They land on the dashed outline. Up to the noise of a finite dataset, D P O has found the R L H F optimum.
run/lossc: The loss falls from zero point six nine three, and settles near zero point four two, not zero.
run/noisy: It cannot reach zero, because the labels are noisy. Even the true reward agrees with only about eighty three percent of them.
recipe/real: On a real language model, the recipe is short.
recipe/seq: The log probability of a whole answer is the sum of the log probabilities of its tokens, each given the ones before. One forward pass computes them all, with the prompt tokens masked out.
recipe/two: Start from the fine tuned model, and make two copies: the policy, which trains, and the reference, which stays frozen.
recipe/pairs: Collect preference pairs once, from people, or from a strong model acting as a judge.
recipe/cache: Since the reference never changes, its log probabilities can even be computed once, ahead of time.
recipe/train: Then train with the D P O loss, usually for one to a few passes, with a small learning rate.
recipe/compare: Compare that with P P O. Four models become two. Sampling at every step becomes none. A long list of settings becomes mostly beta and the learning rate.
recipe/spread: That simplicity is why D P O spread so fast: from Zephyr in late 2023, to Llama 3 in 2024.
limits/same: The strengths and the weaknesses of D P O come from the same place: it never leaves its dataset.
limits/explore: First, it cannot explore. P P O grades the policy's own fresh answers. D P O only sees answers someone else wrote, so once the policy moves, it writes text that nobody ever judged.
limits/online: A common fix is online D P O: generate new pairs from the current model, label them, and train again.
limits/certain: Second, certain preferences break the leash. If every label says A beats B, the loss keeps shrinking as the gap grows.
limits/push: So D P O keeps pushing, and the probability of B races toward zero, whatever beta says.
limits/ipo: I P O replaces the loss with a squared error that aims for a fixed gap, and stops there.
limits/both: Third, the loss only cares about the gap. Often both answers lose probability, the rejected one just faster.
limits/length: And if the chosen answers in the data tend to be longer, the model learns that length itself is rewarded.
limits/kto: Two more variants are worth knowing. K T O needs no pairs at all: just a thumbs up or a thumbs down for each answer.
limits/simpo: Sim P O drops the reference model, and scores answers by their average log probability per token, which also removes the pull toward long answers.
outro/recap: Let us put the five steps side by side.
outro/s1: One: the objective. Expected reward, minus beta times the K L to the reference.
outro/s2: Two: its best policy has a formula. The reference, tilted by e to the reward over beta, and divided by Z.
outro/s3: Three: turned around, any policy implies a reward, up to a constant per prompt.
outro/s4: Four: Bradley-Terry only uses differences, so that constant cancels.
outro/s5: Five: maximum likelihood on the pairs gives the D P O loss. Logistic regression on the implicit reward margin.
outro/grad: Its gradient raises the chosen answer and lowers the rejected one, weighted by how wrong the model still is.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter. You can drag the policy yourself, try to beat pi star, and train the toy with any beta you like.
